## Virtual environments

A virtual environment lets you have several versions of programming languages,
packages, and other programs on the same computer,
kept apart so they do not conflict with each other.
You might have a different environment for each project,
each with its own versions of a language and its packages.

Most virtual environment tools can also share an environment,
which helps make data science projects reproducible:

- the environment is written down,
  so there is a record of which versions the project used
- other people can recreate the same environment on their own computers,
  and reproduce your results from your data and code
- programming languages and their packages change over time,
  with new features and bug fixes that can change how your code runs,
  so a project needs its environment, as well as its data and code,
  to stay reproducible over time

Environments have other benefits too:

- If two of your projects rely on different versions of the same package,
  you can install these in different environments.
- If you want to try a new package,
  you don't have to change the package versions your data analysis uses
  and risk breaking something.
  (Installing a new package can upgrade other packages it shares dependencies with.)
- When you develop your own packages,
  environments are essential,
  because you need to know exactly which packages yours depends on,
  so that it runs on computers other than your own.

There are many virtual environment tools,
even if we only look at R and Python.

For R, the R Works post
[{renv}, {rix}, rv, uvr, ir: An explosion of R package and environment managers](https://rworks.dev/posts/r-managers/)
(Isabella Velásquez, 2026) compares the current options:

- [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/),
  long-established project-local package management, supported by Posit,
  and the one this book uses
- [`rix`](https://docs.ropensci.org/rix/),
  which uses Nix to snapshot a whole software environment:
  R itself, its packages, and the system libraries they need
- [`rv`](https://a2-ai.github.io/rv-docs/),
  newer project-local package management, written in Rust,
  where you declare the packages you want and `rv` resolves them
- [`uvr`](https://nbafrank.github.io/uvr/),
  modeled on Python's `uv`,
  which manages both R packages and R versions with one lockfile
- [`ir`](https://r-lib.github.io/ir/),
  for single scripts and Quarto documents that list their packages inside the file,
  much like `uv add --script` for a Python script
- [`rig`](https://rig.r-lib.org/),
  which installs and switches between R versions,
  something `renv` and `rv` leave to you

Older R projects may also use `packrat`,
which `renv` replaced,
or `conda`.

For Python, the options include:

- [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/),
  a fast package and project manager that also installs Python versions,
  and the one this book uses
- [`venv`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html),
  built into Python,
  which creates an environment that you fill with `pip`
- [`virtualenv`](https://virtualenv.pypa.io/),
  a third-party tool that creates isolated Python environments
- [`conda`](https://docs.conda.io/),
  package, dependency, and environment management for any language,
  including Python and R
- [`mamba`](https://mamba.readthedocs.io/),
  a fast package manager that works with `conda` environments
- [`pixi`](https://pixi.sh/latest/),
  a package manager for conda and PyPI packages, with lockfiles built in
- [`poetry`](https://python-poetry.org/),
  dependency management and packaging, with a `poetry.lock` lockfile
- [`pipenv`](https://pipenv.pypa.io/),
  which combines `pip`, `virtualenv`, and a `Pipfile` in one tool
- [`pyenv`](https://github.com/pyenv/pyenv),
  which installs and switches between Python versions,
  as `rig` does for R

In this book, we use `uv` for Python and `renv` for R:

- **Python with `uv`**, starting
  from [Virtual environments: Python (uv)](0520-virtual-environments-python-uv.qmd)
- **R with `renv`**, starting
  from [Virtual environments: R (renv)](0560-virtual-environments-r-renv.qmd)

Both tie an environment to a project folder,
and both keep the packages a project *declares*
separate from the exact versions it *locks*.

You will also meet `conda` in other projects,
so this part ends with two chapters on it,
[Virtual environments: Python (conda)](0570-virtual-environments-python-conda.qmd)
and [Virtual environments: Python (conda-lock)](0580-virtual-environments-python-conda-lock.qmd).

- `conda` is nice because it works with both R and Python.
- It is less widely adopted in the R community than in Python,
  so fewer R packages are available from it,
  and often at older versions than on CRAN, R's package repository.
- You can make a `conda` package for any R package on CRAN,
  but it takes time and effort, and is sometimes not straightforward.

That is why we use `renv` for R.
It is widely adopted in the R community,
and it works directly with the packages on CRAN,
so you can build environments with the most recent version of any CRAN package,
with less work than `conda`.

:::{.callout-note title="A note on terminology"}
Technically, what this part discusses are *virtual* environments.
In practice we often drop the "virtual" and call them "environments",
in this book and in class.
:::
